timescale__timescaledb@f84194c.pr_summary: Refactors TimescaleDB's RowCompressor and RowDecompressor so they no longer own relations or write state: both are built from TupleDescs (plus CompressionSettings for the compressor), and a new BulkWriter (out_rel, catalog index state, command id captured at build, bulk-insert state, executor state, insert options) performs heap/index inserts. Decompression column mapping uses a name-based AttrMap; the compressor flush is split into row_compressor_build_tuple / row_compressor_clear_batch. Callers (compress_chunk, decompress_chunk, DML decompression, segmentwise recompression, hypercore) are updated and the close functions now free owned arrays and descriptors.

excluded.reason: Claims segmentwise recompression now stamps later segments' compressed inserts with a stale command id captured once in bulk_writer_build (C2, C14, C19). Not a defect with any consequence: the only reader inside recompress_chunk_segmentwise_impl is the index scan over the snapshot registered at recompress.c:318, after the writer is built at :264 with no CCI in between, so snapshot->curcid equals writer.mycid and tuples stamped with it are invisible to that scan exactly as the later-cid tuples were before the PR; deletes (recompress.c:884) only touch tuples returned by that scan, and every later command in the transaction sees all inserts regardless. The DML/decompress path already captured mycid once at build before the PR (base compression.c:1352). A command-id labelling change with no reachable wrong result.

Claims recompression inserts later segments with a stale command id captured once by bulk_writer_build. Same as C2: the scan snapshot's curcid equals the captured id (writer built at recompress.c:264, snapshot at :318, no CCI between), so the inserts stay invisible to it exactly as before and no reachable wrong result follows.

Claims recompression inserts later segments with a stale command id captured once by bulk_writer_build. Same as C2: the scan snapshot's curcid equals the captured id (writer built at recompress.c:264, snapshot at :318, no CCI between), so the inserts stay invisible to it exactly as before and no reachable wrong result follows.

Claims bulk_writer_build's bistate/indexstate/estate leak on ERROR because compress_chunk/decompress_chunk lack PG_TRY cleanup. On ERROR PostgreSQL transaction abort releases buffer pins, relation/index references and memory contexts via resource owners; the pre-PR compressor/decompressor held the same state without PG_TRY, so nothing new leaks.

Claims row_compressor_close should delete per_row_ctx and otherwise leaks it. Pre-existing: the base row_compressor_close never deleted per_row_ctx either; it is a child of the caller's memory context and is freed with it.
Suggests NULLing out_desc after FreeTupleDesc in row_compressor_close for defensive coding. Style only; no caller uses the compressor after close.

Claims build_decompress_attrmap leaves unmatched attnums uninitialised so they may be treated as real attnums. make_attrmap palloc0s attnums, so unmatched entries are 0 = InvalidAttrNumber, and create_per_compressed_column checks AttributeNumberIsValid (compression.c:1583).
Suggests skipping metadata columns early in build_decompress_attrmap to avoid wasted iterations. A micro-optimisation of a one-time mapping loop; no defect.

Claims decompress_batch allocates heap_form_tuple results before switching to per_compressed_row_ctx, leaking them. Wrong: decompress_batch itself switches to per_compressed_row_ctx at entry (compression.c:1714), and this code is unchanged by the PR.

Asks for an assertion that compressed_chunk_rel->rd_id equals settings->fd.compress_relid in recompress. Assertion request; settings come from the chunk (recompress.c:137) whose compress_relid is that compressed chunk, so no mismatch exists.

Claims the BulkWriter in hypercore_decompress_update_segment leaks if decompression throws. Same as R1: error cleanup is done by transaction abort/resource owners, unchanged versus the pre-PR decompressor-owned state.

Asks for an assertion that new_compressed_rel->rd_id equals settings->fd.compress_relid in compress_and_swap_heap. Assertion request; make_new_heap copies the old compressed relation's descriptor so attnums from compress_relid match, and such an Assert would actually fail there.
Claims the BulkWriter in compress_and_swap_heap leaks if row_compressor_append_sorted_rows throws. Same as R1/R8: abort-time resource-owner cleanup; nothing new.
Asks for an assertion that compressed_rel->rd_id equals settings->fd.compress_relid in convert_to_hypercore_finish. Assertion request only; no concrete mismatch is shown.
Asks to rename local attrMap to attrmap/attr_map per the style guide. Naming style preference, not a defect.
Asks to rename attrMap to attr_map per the style guide. Naming style preference, not a defect.

Claims compression.h fails to compile for consumers because it uses AttrMap without including access/attmap.h. compression.h includes catalog/indexing.h, which pulls in nodes/execnodes.h -> access/tupconvert.h -> access/attmap.h, so AttrMap is always declared; every consumer (compression_dml.c, recompress.c, hypercore_handler.c) compiles.
Claims compression.h must include access/attmap.h or consumers fail to compile. Same as C3: AttrMap is available transitively via catalog/indexing.h -> nodes/execnodes.h -> access/tupconvert.h.

Claims recompress.c and hypercore_handler.c will fail to compile because compression.h lacks access/attmap.h. Same as C3: the type is declared transitively through catalog/indexing.h, so there is no build break.

Claims build_column_map resolves attnums from settings->fd.compress_relid but applies them to a possibly different compressed descriptor, putting values in wrong columns. Every caller passes the descriptor of compress_relid itself or of a make_new_heap copy of it (hypercore compress_and_swap_heap), which has identical physical layout; no reachable caller has a differing layout.

Claims row_compressor_init's count-column lookup and build_column_map take offsets from catalog relids rather than the supplied descriptors, so a different-layout caller would misplace columns. Hypothetical future caller; all current callers pass descriptors matching the catalog relations (the commenter concedes the heap-rewrite caller preserves layout).

Suggests the DML path reuse decompressor.count_compressed_attindex instead of looking up the count column itself. Duplication/style suggestion; both lookups resolve the same column and have not drifted.
Suggests compression_dml.c:527 use decompressor.count_compressed_attindex instead of a second lookup. Same as C7: maintainability preference with no divergence.
Asks to document that the tuple returned by row_compressor_build_tuple lives in per_row_ctx until clear_batch. Documentation request; the only caller (row_compressor_flush) uses it correctly.

Claims removing the t_tableOid assignment leaves decompressed tuples with an invalid table OID so tableoid-referencing index expressions evaluate wrongly. heap_multi_insert (via table_multi_insert) sets slots[i]->tts_tableOid and tuple->t_tableOid to the target relation before the index insertion loop runs, so index expressions see the correct OID.

Asks to verify index expressions still get the destination OID after the t_tableOid assignment was removed from decompress_batch. Same as C9: table_multi_insert/heap_multi_insert stamps tts_tableOid on every slot before index tuples are built.
Suggests freeing the AttrMap right after create_per_compressed_column instead of keeping it in the decompressor. Design/refactoring preference; the map is freed in row_decompressor_close, no leak.

Claims count_meta_attnum is only Assert-checked so a missing count column yields a negative index in production. Compressed chunks always carry the count metadata column; before the PR a missing column was not checked at all (index silently 0), so this is contrived and not made worse in a reachable way.

Asks whether decompression's table_multi_insert should honour writer->insert_options instead of 0. Every decompression caller builds the writer with insert_options 0, so behaviour is identical; no consequence.

Suggests not building a BulkWriter (indexes, bistate, estate) for delete-only DML scans. Before the PR build_decompressor opened the same indexes/bistate/estate in delete-only mode, so this is not a regression; optimisation suggestion.
Suggests constructing the BulkWriter only when rows are actually written, not in delete-only scans. Same as C18: pre-existing cost, not made worse.

Suggests passing progress-reporting inputs separately instead of an unrelated in_rel to row_compressor_append_sorted_rows. API design preference; in_rel is only used for reltuples/log name and behaves as before.

timescale__timescaledb@2568b01.pr_summary: Fixes a use-after-free in the Hypercore table access method: HypercoreInfo (rd_amcache) obtained via RelationGetHypercoreInfo() could be freed by invalidation processing inside table_open(), and was then used (e.g. count column attno) during whole-segment DELETE. The PR adds hypercore_open_compressed() to open a chunk's compressed relation, replaces direct table_open(hsinfo->compressed_relid, …) calls with it, and changes whole-segment delete and index-only-scan conversion helpers to take the Relation and fetch HypercoreInfo at the point of use.

defects.title: hypercore_open_compressed ignores its lock mode and always takes AccessShareLock, silently downgrading every DML/CLUSTER lock on the compressed relation
defects.statement: The new helper hypercore_open_compressed(Relation relation, LOCKMODE mode) (tsl/src/hypercore/hypercore_handler.c:105-110) calls `table_open(hcinfo->compressed_relid, AccessShareLock)` instead of `mode`. Every caller that previously requested a stronger lock now only gets AccessShareLock on the compressed relation: hypercore_index_delete_tuples (1550, RowExclusiveLock), hypercore_tuple_delete (1857, RowExclusiveLock — deleting whole compressed segments), hypercore_decompress_update_segment (1939, RowExclusiveLock — deletes/rewrites compressed tuples), hypercore_tuple_lock (2025, RowShareLock) and compress_and_swap_heap (2172, AccessExclusiveLock, used by CLUSTER/VACUUM FULL before make_new_heap/finish_heap_swap of that relation). Tuples are thus deleted/modified in the compressed relation without the table-level lock PostgreSQL's conflict table relies on (e.g. no conflict with a concurrent ShareLock CREATE INDEX on the compressed relation), and the heap swap of the compressed relation proceeds holding only AccessShareLock, allowing concurrent access to a relation whose relfilenode is being swapped. All these sites close with NoLock, so nothing reveals the missing lock.
defects.evidence: head hypercore_handler.c:106-109 `hypercore_open_compressed(Relation relation, LOCKMODE mode) { HypercoreInfo *hcinfo = RelationGetHypercoreInfo(relation); return table_open(hcinfo->compressed_relid, AccessShareLock); }`; base had e.g. `table_open(hsinfo->compressed_relid, RowExclusiveLock)` in hypercore_tuple_delete and `table_open(old_compressed_relid, AccessExclusiveLock)` in compress_and_swap_heap; callers close with `table_close(crel, NoLock)` (1888, 1972, 2046, 2202, 1585).
defects.notes: Must say the `mode` parameter is unused / table_open is hardcoded to AccessShareLock, so callers asking for RowExclusive/RowShare/AccessExclusive get a weaker lock.

excluded.reason: Claims the local `hinfo` in whole_segment_delete_state_create shadows a function parameter and should be inlined. The parameter is now `rel` (hypercore_handler.c:1740), so nothing is shadowed; style only.

Claims the HypercoreInfo pointer fetched at hypercore_handler.c:1751 may be invalidated by later catalog/heap calls before use. Between the fetch and its only use (heap_getattr of count_cattno at ~1775) the function only allocates memory, registers a reset callback, reads and locks a buffer of an already-open relation — none of which processes invalidation messages — so the pointer is valid when used.
Claims the local `hsinfo` in convert_index_only_scans shadows a parameter of the same name. The function now takes `Relation rel` (hypercore_handler.c:3881); no shadowing, style only.

Claims calling RelationGetHypercoreInfo per attribute inside the loop is avoidable overhead and risks invalidation. It returns the cached rd_amcache pointer (cheap) in a planner loop over a few index keys, and nothing in the loop processes invalidations; no concrete consequence.
Claims the RelationGetHypercoreInfo lookup in convert_index_only_scans should be hoisted out of the per-attribute loop. Same as R5: a negligible cached lookup; optimisation nit, not a defect.

Claims the new comment in hypercore_tuple_delete ('fetch the caminfo again here') is stale because no caminfo variable exists there. The comment still correctly explains why HypercoreInfo is re-fetched (inside is_whole_segment_delete/whole_segment_delete_state_create after table_open); wording nit.
Claims the same comment should say whole_segment_delete_state_create does the fresh lookup. Wording nit identical to C1; the comment does not mislead about behaviour.
Asks for a regression test that provokes relcache invalidation before a whole-segment DELETE. A request for tests, not a defect in the change.

timescale__timescaledb@5ab9b12.pr_summary: Removes the early return in get_compressed_chunk_index_for_recompression (tsl/src/compression/api.c) that refused segmentwise recompression for chunks without segmentby columns, so such chunks now use recompress_chunk_segmentwise_impl (whole chunk treated as one segment) instead of decompress+compress. Adds a debug/INFO log line in recompress.c, a regression test for a no-segmentby hypertable, and updates many expected outputs (chunk/hypertable id renumbering).

defects.title: "using non-segmentby index for recompression" is logged unconditionally, misreporting the path for segmentby chunks
defects.statement: The new elog at tsl/src/compression/recompress.c:173 sits outside any num_segmentby check. recompress_chunk_segmentwise_impl serves every segmentwise recompression, including the ordinary segmentby case, so with timescaledb.debug_compression_path_info on it prints an INFO line claiming a non-segmentby index is used even when the segmentby index is used (and the comment above it describes only the no-segmentby case). The diagnostic is inaccurate; it should be guarded by num_segmentby == 0 or name the actual index.
defects.evidence: recompress.c:160 `int num_segmentby = ts_array_length(settings->fd.segmentby);` ... recompress.c:173 `elog(ts_guc_debug_compression_path_info ? INFO : DEBUG1, "using non-segmentby index for recompression") ;` with no condition; the same function is called for segmentby chunks from api.c tsl_compress_chunk_wrapper and recompress_chunk_segmentwise.
defects.notes: A comment must say the log message is misleading/inaccurate: emitted regardless of segmentby, or does not reflect the index actually used. A comment only about the whitespace before the semicolon does not count.

defects.title: Existing full-recompression test now takes the segmentwise path; its comment is wrong and the fallback coverage is lost
defects.statement: The mytab test in tsl/test/sql/recompress_chunk_segmentwise.sql:236-244 re-enables compression with no segmentby and states at :241 'expect to see a different compressed chunk after recompressing now as the operation is decompress + compress'. With the no-segmentby guard removed from api.c, that chunk now takes segmentwise recompression, and the PR simply rebaselined the expected output to the SAME compressed chunk (recompress_chunk_segmentwise.out:486). The test comment is now false, and the test no longer exercises the full-recompression fallback it was written to cover (no other case in the file covers compress_chunk falling back when no usable index exists).
defects.evidence: recompress_chunk_segmentwise.sql:241 `-- expect to see a different compressed chunk after recompressing now as the operation is decompress + compress`; expected output diff changes `compress_hyper_13_14_chunk | compress_hyper_13_15_chunk` to `compress_hyper_13_14_chunk | compress_hyper_13_14_chunk` at .out:486.
defects.notes: A comment must point out that the existing mytab/before-after test (or its comment) now contradicts the new behaviour / no longer tests full recompression. Generic 'add more tests for noseg' requests do not count.

excluded.reason: Claims there is trailing whitespace before the semicolon at recompress.c:173. Pure formatting nit (clang-format would fix it); no functional or maintainability consequence.

Claims a different two-key index on the compressed chunk could be selected instead of the metadata index because get_compressed_chunk_index only checks key count when there is no segmentby. Compressed chunks are internal tables whose indexes are created by TimescaleDB (the default (_ts_meta_min_1,_ts_meta_max_1) index); a second index with the same key count requires a user manually indexing an internal chunk, and the same count-only/orderby-unchecked selection already applies to segmentby chunks (compression.c:658-690, loop skips orderby columns entirely). Contrived and pre-existing.

Claims a user-created index with the same key count on a no-segmentby compressed chunk could be chosen and scanned as if ordered by batch metadata, recompressing against wrong batches. Same as C1: requires hand-made indexes on internal compressed chunks, and get_compressed_chunk_index's weak validation (no orderby-column check) is pre-existing for the segmentby path too; not a realistic path introduced by this PR.

Claims that with no segmentby keys index_rescan restarts an unrestricted scan for each input row, making the path quadratic. Wrong: the outer loop in recompress.c only rescans after done_with_segment, which with zero segmentby keys (check_changed_group never reports a change) happens only when input is exhausted; the matching loop advances batch by batch with a single forward index scan.

Claims compression_chunk_size statistics are not updated by segmentwise recompression, so no-segmentby chunks now undercount. That the segmentwise path does not rewrite compression_chunk_size is existing, deliberate behaviour of segmentwise recompression shared by all segmentby chunks; this PR only routes one more chunk shape through the established path and does not make the mechanism worse.

Claims the compression policy picks segmentwise recompression solely from the index probe and so ignores changed hypertable settings. The policy logic in sql/policy_internal.sql is unchanged and behaves identically for segmentby chunks, where it already did this; recompress uses the compressed chunk's own settings consistently. Pre-existing policy behaviour, not introduced by this PR.
Asks the new noseg test to assert row preservation after recompression. Request for more test coverage, not a defect in the code.
Asks the new noseg test to select and assert the resulting rows after recompression. Test-coverage request, not a defect.
Asks the new test to insert a row inside an existing batch's range and assert the recompressed rows. Test-coverage request, not a defect.

timescale__timescaledb@7148e5c.pr_summary: Adds a refresh_newest_first BOOL (default true) parameter to add_continuous_aggregate_policy (SQL signature plus latest-dev/reverse-dev update scripts), a config key and JSONB getter, a PolicyContinuousAggData field filled in job.c config validation, and threads it into continuous_agg_split_refresh_window, which now orders the batch query ASC or DESC via psprintf. The incremental refresh test passes refresh_newest_first => false for one policy.

defects.title: refresh_newest_first is never read from the SQL call or stored in the job config, so passing false has no effect
defects.statement: The SQL function gains an 11th argument (sql/policy_api.sql:94; also latest-dev.sql:26), but the C entry point policy_refresh_cagg_add (tsl/src/bgw_policy/continuous_aggregate_api.c:689-756) still reads only args 0-9, and policy_refresh_cagg_add_internal (:531-536) has no parameter for it and never writes POL_REFRESH_CONF_KEY_REFRESH_NEWEST_FIRST into the job's JSONB config (:650-663). At run time policy_refresh_cagg_get_refresh_newest_first (:172-181, read at job.c:508) always finds the key missing and returns true. add_continuous_aggregate_policy(..., refresh_newest_first => false) is silently accepted and still refreshes newest-first; the updated expected test output encodes exactly this (batch 1 of 4 is the Mar 11 window, batch 4 the Feb 24 window after the `false` policy), so the test cannot detect it.
defects.evidence: continuous_aggregate_api.c:724-725 `max_batches_per_execution.value = PG_GETARG_DATUM(9); ... PG_ARGISNULL(9);` is the last argument read; the _add_internal call passes no ordering flag; `git grep refresh_newest_first` finds no writer of the config key (only the getter, job.c:508, refresh.c). Expected output after `refresh_newest_first => false` still lists the newest window as batch 1.
defects.notes: A comment must say the new argument is not consumed/persisted by policy_refresh_cagg_add / _add_internal (never written to the job config) so the option is a no-op, OR that the test's expected output still shows newest-first order despite `false` (i.e. the option is ignored). Comments about DROP IF EXISTS, ts_update_placeholder, or the psprintf allocation do not count.

defects.title: With oldest-first order, the NULL-offset unbounded endpoints are attached to the wrong batches
defects.statement: continuous_agg_split_refresh_window now returns batches in ASC order when refresh_newest_first is false (refresh.c:1143-1145), but the batch-building loop still assumes DESC: it gives row i==0 an unbounded end when the policy's end offset is NULL (refresh.c:1222-1226) and the last row an unbounded start when the start offset is NULL (:1233-1237). In ASC order row 0 is the OLDEST batch, so it becomes [oldest_start, +infinity) - overlapping every other batch and refreshing the whole window in the first batch (defeating buckets_per_batch / max_batches_per_execution) - and the newest batch gets a -infinity start. The PR's own test policy uses end_offset => NULL with refresh_newest_first => false (cagg_refresh_policy_incremental.sql:293-301), so this path is hit as soon as the option actually takes effect (today it is reachable by setting the config key via alter_job).
defects.evidence: refresh.c:1145 `psprintf(query_str_template, refresh_newest_first ? "DESC" : "ASC")`; :1222 `if (i == 0 && original_refresh_window->end_isnull) { range->end = ts_time_get_noend_or_max(range->type); ...}`; :1233 `if (i == (SPI_processed - 1) && original_refresh_window->start_isnull) { range->start = ts_time_get_nobegin_or_min(...); }` - positions chosen by list index, not chronology.
defects.notes: A comment must say that in ascending order the first/last batch index no longer corresponds to newest/oldest, so the unbounded end (NULL end_offset) is attached to the oldest batch and/or the unbounded start to the newest. Merely saying the comment about reverse order is stale does not count.

defects.title: The batch-production comment still says batches are always produced newest-first
defects.statement: The explanatory comment above the batch query (refresh.c:1066-1082) states batches are produced in reverse order so the most recent data is processed first; with the new ASC branch (refresh.c:1145) that is now conditional on refresh_newest_first, so the comment is wrong for the new mode.
defects.evidence: refresh.c:1069-1073 'The batches are produced in reverse order ... because the most recent data should be the first to be processed' vs :1145 choosing ASC when refresh_newest_first is false.
defects.notes: A comment must say the reverse-order/newest-first comment is now stale or conditional.

excluded.reason: Claims the update script's DROP FUNCTION without IF EXISTS can fail the migration if the old signature is absent. Update scripts run only from the immediately preceding version, where this exact 10-arg signature exists, and TimescaleDB's own update scripts use plain DROP FUNCTION the same way; the failure state is not reachable in the upgrade path.

Claims latest-dev.sql uses the wrong C symbol 'ts_update_placeholder' instead of 'ts_policy_refresh_cagg_add'. That is the TimescaleDB update-script convention: the placeholder is rebound when the full function definitions (policy_api.sql's CREATE OR REPLACE ... 'ts_policy_refresh_cagg_add') are replayed after the update fragment.
Claims reverse-dev.sql uses the wrong C symbol 'ts_update_placeholder'. Same convention as R2: downgrade scripts' placeholder bodies are replaced when the target version's definitions are applied.

Claims policy_refresh_cagg_get_refresh_newest_first may crash on a NULL config. The config passed is always the job's config (as for the sibling getters buckets_per_batch / max_batches_per_execution with the same assumption); speculative, not reachable.

Claims the refresh_newest_first read in job.c:508 should be moved inside `if (policy_data)` for performance. A single cheap JSONB lookup mirroring how every other field is read there; no measurable cost, style only.

Claims the psprintf in refresh.c:1145 can accumulate memory in a long-lived context. It runs once per policy execution inside the job transaction's memory context, which is reset afterwards; no accumulation in practice.

unionlabs__union@d840723.pr_summary: Introduces a `Timestamp(u64)` nanosecond newtype in voyager-core (from_nanos/from_secs/as_nanos/as_secs, Display) and replaces the raw integer timestamps with it: `ConsensusStateMeta.timestamp_nanos`, `WaitForTimestamp.timestamp` (was i64), and the return type of the `queryLatestTimestamp` RPC on both the ConsensusModule and VoyagerRpc traits and the server (was i64). All client, consensus and state modules and the ethereum client-update plugin are updated to wrap their values with Timestamp::from_nanos / from_secs.

defects.title: Ethereum and Movement consensus/state modules wrap non-nanosecond values (seconds, microseconds) in Timestamp::from_nanos, so the new 'nanoseconds' type lies and WaitForTimestamp comparisons against those chains are off by 1e9 / 1e3
defects.statement: The PR's stated goal is a single nanosecond timestamp type, and it adds Timestamp::from_secs for exactly this purpose (used in voyager/plugins/client-update/ethereum/src/main.rs:539), and the Ethereum bootstrap already normalises the same execution timestamp to nanos (voyager/modules/client-bootstrap/ethereum/src/main.rs:243 `* 1_000_000_000`). But voyager/modules/consensus/ethereum/src/main.rs:167-195 feeds the execution-payload `timestamp` (beacon finalized_header.execution.timestamp and the alloy block header timestamp, both Unix SECONDS) into Timestamp::from_nanos, and voyager/modules/consensus/movement/src/main.rs:165 and voyager/modules/state/movement/src/main.rs:148 feed Aptos `block_timestamp` (MICROSECONDS; hubble/src/indexer/aptos/block_handle.rs:36 multiplies it by 1000 to get nanos) into Timestamp::from_nanos. Call::WaitForTimestamp (lib/voyager-message/src/call.rs:238) compares the queried Timestamp with a target built in nanoseconds, so any wait targeting an Ethereum or Movement chain would consider the timestamp never reached. The numeric values are unchanged from before the PR (it was already a unit mix behind a raw i64), so this is an incomplete conversion rather than a new runtime regression; the only current WaitForTimestamp producer waits on the counterparty (cometbls/tendermint, true nanos).
defects.evidence: ethereum: `Ok(Timestamp::from_nanos(self.beacon_api_client.finality_update()...data.finalized_header.execution.timestamp,)` (execution payload timestamp, lib/beacon-api-types/src/execution_payload_header.rs:29 `pub timestamp: u64`, Unix seconds) and `Timestamp::from_nanos(...header.timestamp.try_into().unwrap())`; movement: `let timestamp = block.inner().block_timestamp.0; ... Ok(Timestamp::from_nanos(timestamp).try_into().unwrap())`; hubble aptos: `OffsetDateTime::from_unix_timestamp_nanos(block_timestamp * 1000)`; lib/voyager-core/src/lib.rs:335 `pub fn from_secs(secs: u64) -> Self` exists but is not used here.
defects.notes: Must say the ethereum value is seconds and/or the movement (Aptos) value is microseconds, and wrapping it with from_nanos is the wrong unit. Merely saying `.try_into()` is redundant does not count.

defects.title: TODO comments saying the timestamp should return 'a better type than i64' are left in place after the PR changed the type to Timestamp
defects.statement: The PR replaces the i64 return type with Timestamp but keeps the now-obsolete TODOs directly above the changed signatures: lib/voyager-message/src/module.rs:442 and lib/voyager-message/src/rpc.rs:41 (`// TODO: Make this return a better type than i64`), voyager/modules/consensus/movement/src/main.rs:146 (same text), and `// TODO: Use a better timestamp type here` in the cometbls (main.rs:130), ethereum (main.rs:159) and tendermint (main.rs:123) consensus modules and the movement state module (main.rs:133). They now describe work that this PR has done, misleading readers.
defects.evidence: module.rs:442-443 `// TODO: Make this return a better type than i64` / `async fn query_latest_timestamp(&self, finalized: bool) -> RpcResult<Timestamp>;`
defects.notes: Must say a TODO about i64 / a better timestamp type is stale now that Timestamp is returned (any of the listed sites).

excluded.reason: Suggests deriving Copy/Default and #[serde(transparent)] on Timestamp for wire compatibility. Ergonomics suggestion. serde_json serializes a derived newtype struct `Timestamp(u64)` as its bare inner number (serialize_newtype_struct), and deserializes it from a number, so the JSON wire format is already identical to the old integer; #[serde(transparent)] is not needed for correctness. Copy/Default are nice-to-haves.
Suggests implementing From<u64>/Into<u64> for Timestamp. Style: adding From<u64>/Into<u64> impls is an API preference, not a defect.

Claims Timestamp::from_secs can overflow on secs * 1_000_000_000. `secs * 1_000_000_000` overflows only above ~1.8e10 seconds (year 2554). The only caller (client-update/ethereum main.rs:539) passes genesis_time + slots*seconds_per_slot, a current Unix time; the old code multiplied the same way. Unreachable in practice.

Claims changing the queryLatestTimestamp return type to Timestamp breaks the RPC (units, signedness, JSON shape, missing JsonSchema). Timestamp serializes as a bare JSON number (newtype struct), so the RPC shape is unchanged; values were already nanoseconds per the old `/// THIS IS NANOSECONDS` doc on WaitForTimestamp and the cometbls/tendermint implementations; no negative timestamps are produced. No JsonSchema bound exists on this RPC return type (the workspace compiles without it).

Claims the Timestamp return type changes the JSON-RPC wire format of queryLatestTimestamp. Same as R5: derived newtype serializes as the bare number in JSON; the modules and voyager are built from the same workspace; no wire break.
Suggests logging latest_timestamp via Display instead of as_nanos(). Logging style preference; `latest_timestamp = latest_timestamp.as_nanos()` is correct.

Claims `.try_into().expect(...)` after Timestamp::from_nanos in cometbls is redundant and incorrect. The redundant `.try_into()` is the identity TryFrom<T> for T (Infallible); it compiles and cannot fail. Style only.

Claims the `.expect()` on the cometbls timestamp conversion can panic at runtime. After the change the `.try_into()` is Timestamp->Timestamp with error type Infallible, so the `.expect()` can never panic; before the PR the u64->i64 conversion could, so the PR removed rather than added a panic.

Claims the unwraps in the ethereum query_latest_timestamp can panic. The unwraps on the Timestamp conversion and u64->u64 try_into are infallible; the `.unwrap().unwrap()` on get_block is pre-existing and untouched in substance.
Claims the `.try_into().unwrap()` after Timestamp::from_nanos in movement consensus is an unnecessary double conversion. Redundant identity conversion; compiles and is infallible. Style.
Claims `expect("should be fine")` in tendermint can panic and crash. The `.expect("should be fine")` is now on an Infallible identity conversion and cannot panic.
Claims `.try_into().unwrap()` in movement state is unnecessary and could panic. Redundant but harmless identity `.try_into().unwrap()` (Infallible); no runtime risk. Style.

Asks to ensure the movement RPC contract guarantees nanoseconds or rename the variable. It only asks to 'ensure' the unit without identifying that Aptos block_timestamp is microseconds, so it does not identify D1; a vague request, not a finding.

Claims the NANOS_PER_SECOND import in client-update/ethereum is now unused. NANOS_PER_SECOND (client-update/ethereum main.rs:28) is indeed now unused, but that is only an unused-import warning: the workspace does not deny warnings (no .cargo config, workspace lints only deny disallowed_types; crane clippy runs without -D warnings). Trivial cleanup, no build break.

Asks to drop the identity `try_into().expect(...)` after Timestamp::from_nanos in tendermint. Timestamp::from_nanos returns Timestamp, so `.try_into()` is the identity TryFrom<T> for T with Infallible error: it compiles and cannot fail. Redundant-code style only.

Asks to drop the identity `try_into().expect(...)` after Timestamp::from_nanos in cometbls. Timestamp::from_nanos returns Timestamp, so `.try_into()` is the identity TryFrom<T> for T with Infallible error: it compiles and cannot fail. Redundant-code style only.

Claims from_secs's `secs * 1_000_000_000` overflows for large inputs and should be checked. Overflow needs secs > ~1.8e10 (year 2554); the only caller (client-update/ethereum main.rs:539) passes a current Unix time, as the old inline multiplication did. Unreachable in practice.

Asks from_secs to reject or document seconds beyond the nanosecond range. Overflow needs secs > ~1.8e10 (year 2554); the only caller (client-update/ethereum main.rs:539) passes a current Unix time, as the old inline multiplication did. Unreachable in practice.

Claims the NANOS_PER_SECOND import in client-update/ethereum main.rs:28 is now unused. True, but it is only an unused-import warning; the workspace does not deny warnings, so no build break. Trivial cleanup.

Asks from_secs to reject inputs above u64::MAX / 1e9 because the multiplication wraps. Overflow needs secs > ~1.8e10 (year 2554); the only caller (client-update/ethereum main.rs:539) passes a current Unix time, as the old inline multiplication did. Unreachable in practice.

Asks to return the constructed Timestamp directly instead of an identity `try_into().expect(...)` across modules. Timestamp::from_nanos returns Timestamp, so `.try_into()` is the identity TryFrom<T> for T with Infallible error: it compiles and cannot fail. Redundant-code style only.

langflow-ai__langflow@bcfe6f9.pr_summary: Introduces a langflow.serialization package with a unified dispatcher-based serialize() (string/list truncation via MAX_TEXT_LENGTH/MAX_ITEMS_LENGTH moved to serialization/constants.py) and replaces ResultDataResponse._serialize_and_truncate, graph.utils.serialize_field, schema.serialize.recursive_serialize_or_str and Log.serialize_message with it; switches the Pinecone component to a lazily imported PineconeVectorStore; adds property tests for the serializer.

defects.title: Strings are never truncated: the primitive fast path returns every str before the truncating str case
defects.statement: _serialize_dispatcher calls _serialize_primitive first (serialization.py:129-131), which returns any str unchanged (serialization.py:89-90); the only truncating branch `case str(): return _serialize_str(...)` (serialization.py:134-135) is dead. ResultDataResponse.serialize_results/serialize_model (api/v1/schemas.py:273,280-283), which previously cut strings to MAX_TEXT_LENGTH, now return arbitrarily long outputs/logs/messages/artifacts in full, removing the response-size cap. The PR's own tests (test_api_schemas.py test_result_data_response_truncation / test_vertex_build_response_with_long_data, which always generate >50-char text and assert '...' in serialize(long_string, max_length=50); test_serialization.py test_string_serialization for long examples) fail.
defects.evidence: serialization.py:89 `if obj is None or isinstance(obj, int | float | bool | complex | str): return obj`; :130 `if primitive is not None: ... return primitive`; :134 `case str(): return _serialize_str(obj, max_length, max_items)` unreachable. Removed schemas.py code did `if isinstance(obj, str): if len(obj) > max_length: return f"{obj[:max_length]}... [truncated]"`. test_api_schemas.py:20-32 draws st.text(min_size=51) and asserts `"..." in truncated` where truncated = serialize(long_string, max_length=50).
defects.notes: Must say that str values short-circuit through the primitive/early-return path so max_length is never applied (long strings returned in full, response cap lost, or the truncation tests fail). R7 (None-vs-not-primitive sentinel ambiguity) and R6 (claims _serialize_str returns None) do not count.

defects.title: Generic instance catch-all shadows the numpy dtype handling (and Enum branch): NumPy scalars serialize as strings
defects.statement: `case object() if not isinstance(obj, type)` (serialization.py:160-161) matches every instance not handled earlier and returns str(obj). The later Enum/TypeVar/alias cases (162-167) and the numpy dtype handling in `case _` (168-182) can only ever see classes. np.int64, np.uint64, np.float32, np.bool_, np.complex64 are not Python int/float/bool/complex subclasses, so serialize(np.int64(42)) returns '42' and np.bool_(True) 'True': the PR's new numpy handling is dead code and its own test_numpy_int64_serialization / test_numpy_numeric_serialization (test_serialization.py:248-281) fail deterministically, turning the unit-test job red. (The replaced graph-path serialize_field also stringified these values via str(value), so the product-facing wire type is not newly changed there; the defect is the unreachable branch plus the failing tests.)
defects.evidence: serialization.py:160 `case object() if not isinstance(obj, type):  # Match any instance that's not a class` -> `_serialize_instance` = `str(obj)`; :162 `case object() if hasattr(obj, "_name_"):  # Enum case`; :170-172 `if hasattr(obj, "dtype"): if np.issubdtype(obj.dtype, np.number) ...: return obj.item()`. test_serialization.py:252 `assert result == 42` for np.int64(42).
defects.notes: Counts: the match-arm order makes the numpy/Enum/TypeVar/alias branches unreachable for instances (swallowed by the generic object() case), or NumPy scalars become strings / numpy tests fail. A comment only about returning raw class objects is D3. Pure style remarks about the match statement do not count.

defects.title: serialize() returns non-JSON values unchanged (class objects, complex numbers), breaking json.dumps in dict_to_codeblock and the class-serialization tests
defects.statement: A class such as `int` or a user class is a `type`, so it skips the catch-all at serialization.py:160, matches none of 162-167 and reaches `return obj` at 183; serialize() then returns the raw class because `result is not None` (209-210) precedes its own `isinstance(obj, type)` string branch (213-216). complex values are likewise returned by the primitive path (89). dict_to_codeblock (vertex_types.py:481-484) then passes them to json.dumps, which raises TypeError where the removed serialize_field returned str(value). The PR's test_class_serialization, test_builtin_type_serialization and test_nested_class_serialization fail deterministically.
defects.evidence: serialization.py:183 `return obj`; :209 `if result is not None: return result` before :213 `if isinstance(obj, type): ... return str(obj)`. vertex_types.py:482-483 `serialized = {key: serialize(val) ...}; json_str = json.dumps(serialized, indent=4)`. Removed graph/utils.py serialize_field ended with `return str(value)`. test_serialization.py:200-201 `assert serialize(int) == repr(int)`.
defects.notes: Counts: serialize can return a non-JSON-serializable object (raw class, complex, 'fallback returns the original object') so json.dumps in dict_to_codeblock raises TypeError, or class serialization returns the class instead of its string. The numpy-scalar-as-string issue is D2.

defects.title: serialize()'s presentation limits become defaults for non-presentation paths (run results, vertex-build history, artifacts, chat code blocks)
defects.statement: serialize() defaults to max_length=MAX_TEXT_LENGTH, max_items=MAX_ITEMS_LENGTH (serialization.py:186-189). The replaced serialize_field / recursive_serialize_or_str never truncated, but the new call sites pass no limits: ResultData.serialize_results (graph/schema.py:26-27, flow-run results returned to API clients), log_vertex_build data/artifacts (graph/utils.py:163-165, persisted history), artifact _to_list_of_dicts (schema/artifact.py:59), build_output_logs (schema/schema.py:113) and dict_to_codeblock (vertex_types.py:482). Lists longer than 1000 items are now silently cut and get a '... [truncated N items]' string element appended (and strings would be cut at 20000 once D1 is fixed), losing data in results that previously stayed complete.
defects.evidence: serialization.py:188-189 `max_length: int | None = MAX_TEXT_LENGTH, max_items: int | None = MAX_ITEMS_LENGTH`; :80-83 list truncation appends `f"... [truncated {len(obj) - max_items} items]"`. graph/schema.py:26 `return {key: serialize(val) for key, val in value.items()}` (was serialize_field, which recursed lists without any cap).
defects.notes: Counts: a comment that one of these non-API call sites now inherits the default 20000/1000 limits and silently truncates data that serialize_field/recursive_serialize_or_str kept whole (any of the listed sites). Not: complaints about the truncation marker format in the API response path (pre-existing there).

defects.title: Aware datetimes are relabelled to UTC instead of converted, shifting the instant in graph results and output logs
defects.statement: _serialize_datetime does `obj.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).isoformat()` (serialization.py:37), which keeps the wall-clock time and swaps the offset, so 12:00+02:00 becomes 12:00+00:00 (two hours off). The replaced serialize_field and recursive_serialize_or_str used obj.isoformat(), preserving the instant; graph ResultData, vertex-build history and array output logs (schema/schema.py:113) now carry wrong timestamps for offset-aware values. (The ResultDataResponse path already used replace() before this PR.)
defects.evidence: serialization.py:37 `return obj.replace(tzinfo=timezone.utc).isoformat()`; removed schema/serialize.py `if isinstance(obj, datetime): return obj.isoformat()`; removed graph/utils.py `if hasattr(value, "isoformat"): return value.isoformat()`.
defects.notes: Counts: replace(tzinfo=utc) changes the offset without converting the time (should use astimezone) for aware datetimes. Must be about aware/non-UTC datetimes.

defects.title: DataFrame/Series cells are only truncated, not recursively serialized, leaving non-JSON values (Timestamps, UUIDs, bytes) in the output
defects.statement: _serialize_dataframe/_serialize_series (serialization.py:108-121) apply _truncate_value (99-105) and return to_dict(), so object cells such as pd.Timestamp, UUID, Decimal or bytes pass through raw, unlike the recursive dict/list path. The removed serialize_field turned a DataFrame into str(df); now log_vertex_build (graph/utils.py:163) stores records containing e.g. Timestamps in a JSON column, which cannot encode them, so the vertex-build log for such a result fails (swallowed by log_vertex_build's except).
defects.evidence: serialization.py:112-113 `obj = obj.apply(lambda x: x.apply(lambda y: _truncate_value(y, max_length, max_items)))` / `return obj.to_dict(orient="records")` - no serialize() on cell values.
defects.notes: Counts: DataFrame/Series cells are not passed through serialize(), so non-JSON cell values survive. Not: complaints that DataFrame truncation lacks a marker (excluded).

defects.title: Bytes are truncated by byte count before decoding, contradicting the old response behaviour and the PR's own property test
defects.statement: _serialize_bytes slices obj[:max_length] before decode(errors='ignore') and tests len(obj) in bytes (serialization.py:26-31). The removed ResultDataResponse helper decoded first and limited characters. Multibyte text is cut short (possibly mid-character, silently dropped), and >max_length invalid/multibyte bytes produce '...' when the decoded text is short, so test_bytes_serialization (test_serialization.py:64-72, which compares decoded character length) fails whenever hypothesis draws such input.
defects.evidence: serialization.py:28-29 `obj[:max_length].decode("utf-8", errors="ignore") + "..." if len(obj) > max_length`; test :67-70 `decoded = data.decode(...); if len(decoded) > MAX_TEXT_LENGTH: expected = decoded[:MAX_TEXT_LENGTH] + "..."`.
defects.notes: Counts: bytes limit is applied to raw bytes before decoding (unit mismatch vs characters / vs the test).

defects.title: serialize() swallows every error into '[Unserializable Object]', making Log's str fallbacks and the to_str/serialize_or_str contract dead
defects.statement: serialize() catches all exceptions and returns '[Unserializable Object]' (serialization.py:235-237). Log.serialize_message (services/tracing/schema.py:19-24) now wraps serialize() with UnicodeDecodeError/PydanticSerializationError handlers that fall back to str(value), but those can no longer fire, so a log message whose model_dump fails is replaced by the opaque marker instead of its string form as before. Likewise the documented to_str behaviour ('return a string representation if serialization fails', 202) and serialize_or_str's docstring (244) are false: failures return the marker regardless of to_str.
defects.evidence: serialization.py:235-237 `except Exception as e: ... return "[Unserializable Object]"`; tracing/schema.py `return serialize(value)` / `except UnicodeDecodeError: return str(value)` / `except PydanticSerializationError: return str(value)`.
defects.notes: Counts: serialize's catch-all makes the caller's fallback handlers dead / to_str or serialize_or_str does not deliver its documented string fallback.

defects.title: Log messages lose jsonable_encoder's structured conversion: sets (and similar) become str(obj)
defects.statement: Log.serialize_message previously ended with jsonable_encoder(value), which turns sets/frozensets, dataclasses, Paths etc. into JSON structures. It now calls serialize() (tracing/schema.py:20), whose instance catch-all (serialization.py:160-161) returns str(obj) for them, so a log {'tags': {'a','b'}} is exposed as the string "{'a', 'b'}" instead of a list.
defects.evidence: Removed line `value = jsonable_encoder(value)`; new `return serialize(value)`; serialization.py has no set/dataclass case, :160 falls back to str(obj).
defects.notes: Counts: Log.message values that jsonable_encoder structured (sets etc.) are now stringified.

excluded.reason: Claims re-raising the missing-langchain-pinecone ImportError as ValueError breaks callers expecting ImportError. The component's build errors are surfaced as messages; no caller catches ImportError here and langchain-pinecone==0.2.2 is a pinned dependency (pyproject.toml:86) - an exception-type preference, not a defect.

Claims switching from Pinecone to PineconeVectorStore may not accept the same constructor args. The repo pins langchain-pinecone==0.2.2 (pyproject.toml:86), where Pinecone is an alias of PineconeVectorStore with the same parameters; speculative.

Claims build_output_logs loses the old str() fallback for unserializable items because serialize requires to_str=True. Instances already fall back to str(obj) via the catch-all at serialization.py:160-161, so array logs still get strings; only raw classes differ (D3), which this comment does not identify.
Claims _serialize_str returns None for strings longer than max_length. Wrong: serialization.py:21 returns obj[:max_length] + '...'; the real problem is that it is never reached (D1).

Claims _serialize_primitive's None return is ambiguous between 'None primitive' and 'not a primitive'. Harmless: None is handled before the call (serialization.py:127-128); readability only and does not notice str short-circuiting truncation (D1).

Claims the numpy object-dtype branch's recursive serialize call omits max_length/max_items. That branch (serialization.py:181-182) is unreachable for instances (D2) and the unwrapped item is a scalar; no concrete consequence.
Asks that DataFrame head(max_items) truncation be marked like list truncation. Presentation preference for new code; no functional defect.
Asks that _truncate_value mark truncated DataFrame cells. Presentation preference; no functional defect.

Claims the list truncation sentinel string breaks the element contract of record arrays. The same sentinel was appended by the removed ResultDataResponse._serialize_and_truncate; not introduced here (the new-call-site aspect is D4).

Claims importing langflow.serialization.constants eagerly imports numpy/pandas/LangChain into lightweight utilities. Those packages are already loaded by langflow, there is no import cycle, and no concrete consequence is shown.
Claims test_result_data_response_truncation discards serialize_model() and asserts on a separate call. Test-quality request; the test in fact fails due to D1.
Claims the ResultDataResponse test asserts on a standalone serializer call rather than the response. Test-quality request, not a product defect.
Claims the response truncation test checks an independent serialize call instead of response.serialize_model(). Test-quality request, not a product defect.
Claims test_vertex_build_response_with_long_data never inspects the dumped response. Test-quality request, not a product defect.
Asks to remove duplicated embedding branches in Float32Embeddings. That code (pinecone.py:110+) is untouched by this PR and behaviour is identical; style.

Claims ResultData results now keep native number/bool types while the frontend TS types declare strings. TS types are not runtime checks and JSON numbers render fine; speculative, no demonstrated break.
Claims removing MAX_TEXT_LENGTH/MAX_ITEMS_LENGTH from langflow.utils.constants may break saved custom components. No in-tree importer remains and no external use is shown; speculative.
Claims Log serialization now keeps None fields that model_dump(exclude_none=True) used to omit. Extra null keys in a log payload have no demonstrated consumer impact; cosmetic.

langflow-ai__langflow@b1cbdba.pr_summary: Codeflash micro-optimisation of update_target_handle / set_new_target_handle in src/backend/base/langflow/graph/graph/utils.py: the proxy lookup is cached in a local, the generator+next() node search becomes a for/break loop, node['data']['node'] and the template field's proxy dict are cached in locals, and the inputTypes walrus becomes a plain assignment. Behaviour is unchanged.

excluded.reason: Suggests using a walrus `if proxy := target_handle.get('proxy'):` instead of a separate assignment. Style preference; behaviour identical.

Claims indexing node_data['template'][field]['proxy'] when 'flow' is truthy introduces a KeyError/TypeError path. Pre-existing: the base code indexed node['data']['node']['template'][field]['proxy']['field'/'id'] unconditionally under the same condition; the PR only caches that lookup, so no new failure path exists.
Asks to revert the inputTypes two-step assignment back to a walrus. Style preference; no behaviour change.
